PEZA v. Edison Congeneration (October 23, 2009): SC ruled that 'parties cannot refuse to comply with the arbitration clause embedded in their agreements, on the ground of the alleged invalidity of the main contract. Under the principle of separability, an arbitration clause is deemed independent and autonomous of the main contract.'

Why arbitration matters: 'Arbitration is the only method of settling controversies in which the litigants can choose their own judges and craft the rules to be used in deciding their own disputes. It is akin to privatizing the courts, a concept that is in keeping with the international development of trade and industry.'

International recognition: 17 arbitration centers in the Asia-Pacific; PDRCI as pioneer member of the Asia Pacific Regional Arbitration Group (2004, Sydney); cooperation agreements with Korean Commercial Arbitration Board, Indian Council of Arbitration, Indonesian National Board of Arbitration, Singapore International Arbitration Center, Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, and the Institute of Arbitrators and Mediators of Australia

stances.claim: Arbitration is 'akin to privatizing the courts' -- the parties choose their own judges and craft their own procedural rules, and the resulting award is final and unappealable to the judiciary (except via certiorari for grave abuse of discretion). The SC's almost invariable upholding of arbitration agreements and awards encourages the use of arbitration as a court-decongesting mechanism.

stances.confidence: asserted as CJP's governing description of arbitration

stances.claim: The PDRCI's new permanent office in the McKinley Town Center symbolizes institutional permanence -- a landmark that signals to the international arbitration community that PDRCI is a stable, reliable partner. The office is not just physical space but an institutional statement.

stances.confidence: asserted as the ceremonial governing interpretation

notable_anecdotes: PEZA v. Edison separability: the SC ruled that parties cannot refuse to comply with an arbitration clause by claiming the main contract is invalid -- 'under the principle of separability, an arbitration clause is deemed independent and autonomous of the main contract.' This is the legal foundation that makes arbitration clauses enforceable even when the underlying contract is disputed.

Dr. Andrew Tan's floor donation: Alliance Global's chairman donated 'this entire floor in this new landmark, the Trade and Commerce Building, in the newest commercial hub of our country, the McKinley Town Center of Fort Bonifacio Global City' -- making PDRCI's first permanent home possible.

PDRCI's 1976 roots: started as the 'Committee on Arbitration that the PCCI created in 1976 during the presidency of Mr. Fred Elizalde' -- a 35-year journey from a committee to an internationally recognized arbitration center with its own permanent home.

one_paragraph_summary: Delivered June 16, 2011 as the welcome address at the inauguration of the PDRCI's new permanent office at the McKinley Town Center, Fort Bonifacio -- CJP as PDRCI Board of Trustees Chairman -- this address welcomes Justice Jose Portugal Perez (keynote speaker; supports arbitration; the SC 'almost always upholds the validity of agreements to arbitrate as well as the finality of arbitral awards'); Ambassador Francis Chua (PCCI President, whose organization helped locate the new office and from whose 1976 Committee on Arbitration under Fred Elizalde PDRCI traces its roots); and Dr. Andrew Tan (Alliance Global/Megaworld chairman who 'generously donated to PCCI this entire floor in the new landmark Trade and Commerce Building in McKinley Town Center'). The SC's October 23, 2009 ruling in PEZA v. Edison Congeneration is cited: parties cannot refuse to comply with an arbitration clause on the ground of the alleged invalidity of the main contract -- 'under the principle of separability, an arbitration clause is deemed independent and autonomous of the main contract.' CJP defines arbitration's unique advantage: 'Arbitration is the only method of settling controversies in which the litigants can choose their own judges and craft the rules to be used in deciding their own disputes. It is akin to privatizing the courts.' PDRCI's international stature: co-founded the Asia Pacific Regional Arbitration Group in 2004 (Sydney, with 16 other centers); cooperation agreements with the Korean Commercial Arbitration Board, Indian Council of Arbitration, Indonesian National Board of Arbitration, Singapore International Arbitration Center, Hong Kong International Arbitration Centre, and the Institute of Arbitrators and Mediators of Australia. He closes: 'this office marks a distinct milestone, for it symbolizes the permanence of PDRCI as an institution dedicated to the fast and efficient settlement of disputes.'
